title: Trade Liberalization, Intermediate Inputs, and Productivity: Evidence from Indonesia
research_question: How does reducing tariffs on final goods versus reducing tariffs on intermediate inputs affect firm-level productivity in a developing economy? In particular, do firms that import their intermediate inputs experience larger productivity gains from input tariff reductions than firms that do not import, and how do these gains compare to those from output tariff reductions that intensify import competition?
data_description: The primary data source is the Indonesian Manufacturing Survey of Large and Medium-Sized Firms (Survei Industri, SI), an annual census of all manufacturing plants with 20 or more employees, covering 1991–2001. The unit of observation is the plant-year, yielding an unbalanced panel of roughly 15,000 firms per year and 170,741 observations. Plant-level variables include output, employment, capital stock, domestic and imported intermediate inputs (with rupiah expenditures by individual input available for 1998), exports, imports, and foreign ownership. Output and inputs are deflated using five-digit industry producer price indices, with separate deflators for domestic and imported intermediate inputs. Tariff data come from the Indonesian Industry and Trade Department at the HS nine-digit level, aggregated to five-digit ISIC industries (288 industries). Input tariffs are constructed as cost-share-weighted averages of output tariffs using 1998 plant-level input mixes.
institutional_context: Indonesia undertook substantial trade liberalization during the 1990s, with the largest tariff reductions beginning in 1995 following its January 1995 accession to the WTO, which committed it to reduce all bound tariffs to 40 percent or less over ten years (subject to an exclusion list). Average final goods tariffs fell from about 21 percent in 1991 to 8 percent in 2001, while input tariffs fell from about 14 percent to 6 percent, with wide variation across and within industries and an escalating structure (lower tariffs on inputs, higher on final goods). Industries that started with the highest tariffs experienced the largest cuts. Evidence indicates that political connections did not significantly shape tariff rates in Indonesia, mitigating endogeneity concerns. The sample period also encompasses the 1997–1998 Asian financial crisis, during which the rupiah depreciated sharply, raising imported input prices.
